meaning: The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu

phonemes.desc: Initial character of the restored form Narasiṃha.
Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Sanskrit tradition.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NARASIMHA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: नरसिंह (narasiṃha) — nara 'man' + siṃha 'lion'; the compound names the avatāra's hybrid body

kin.label: Pali
kin.form: Narasiha — the Middle Indic form of the name used in Pali commentarial literature

kin.label: Sinhala
kin.form: Siṃhala 'lion(-abode)', source of the island name Ceylon/Sri Lanka — a living cognate of siṃha, 'lion'

kin.label: Modern descendants
kin.form: Narasiṃha, Narasingh, Narasimhudu — the name survives across North and South Indian languages and as a male given name

pronunciation.note: Narasiṃha is Tier 1: the anusvāra (ṃ) in siṃha — the nasal mark Sanskrit writes above the letter — is a distinctive feature the ASCII form narasimha deletes outright. The restoration recovers the exact scholarly transliteration.

domains.title: Man-Lion Avatar
domains.subtitle: Man-Lion Avatar
domains.lead: Narasiṃha is Viṣṇu's man-lion avatāra, the fourth descent of the preserver god, who answered a tyrant's loophole-perfect boon with a form neither man nor beast. Worshipped across India as the god of twilight and the guardian of every threshold, he embodies divine ferocity governed by devotion.

cards.name: Man-Lion Avatar
cards.desc: The central domain: Viṣṇu's fourth avatāra — the form no clause of the tyrant's boon could exclude.

cards.name: The Man-Lion
cards.desc: Nara-siṃha, 'man-lion': nara 'man' + siṃha 'lion' — the hybrid the boon never imagined.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Narasiṃha recovers the anusvāra (ṃ) that plain ASCII deletes — the nasal mark the Sanskrit tradition writes.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested across the Purāṇic corpus — Bhāgavata 7, Viṣṇu 1.17–20, Narasimha Purāṇa — and in temple epigraphy from the Gupta age onward.

symbols.name: The man-lion form
symbols.meaning: The theriomorphic body that defeats the boon: leonine mane and claws joined to human torso and intelligence.

symbols.name: Claws (nakha)
symbols.meaning: Neither weapon nor hand — the talons that honor the letter of the boon while breaking its intent; the nails themselves are hymned (nakhastuti).

symbols.name: The pillar (stambha)
symbols.meaning: The palace column that conceals the god; in theology, the stambha is the imperishable inner support of all beings.

symbols.name: Twilight (sandhyā)
symbols.meaning: Neither day nor night — the loophole hour at which the law of the boon is honored and destroyed at once.

symbols.name: The serene child
symbols.meaning: Prahlāda standing unafraid beside the killer — devotion as the one power the man-lion will always answer.

symbols.name: Eighteen-armed Ugra form
symbols.meaning: The ferocious iconography of the killing: multiple arms, bulging eyes, mane aflame, the tyrant stretched across the thighs.

mythology.lead: The stories of Narasiṃha tell how Viṣṇu defeated a loophole-perfect boon: neither man nor beast could kill the tyrant, so the god came as both at once — a man-lion bursting from a palace pillar at twilight, on a threshold, with claws. The Purāṇic cycle turns on the devotion of the tyrant's own son.

myths.title: The Boon of Hiraṇyakaśipu
myths.text: Hiraṇyakaśipu, king of the daityas, performed austerities so severe that Brahmā offered him a boon. Suspicious of every loophole, the demon stipulated that he should not die by day or night, indoors or outdoors, on earth or in the sky, by weapon or by hand, by man or beast, by god, demon, or nāga. Granted near-invulnerability, he conquered the three worlds and forbade the very name of Viṣṇu — commanding his own subjects, on pain of death, to worship him alone. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (7.3) makes the stipulation a masterpiece of conditional theology: Hiraṇyakaśipu does not ask for immortality, which Brahmā cannot give, but for a contract so airtight that only the maker of loopholes could breach it. His blasphemy completes his doom, for by banning Viṣṇu's name from his own household he makes his own son — the boy Prahlāda, who loves the banned god from the womb — the hinge on which the entire boon will turn.

myths.title: Prahlāda, the Devotee
myths.text: Prahlāda, the tyrant's son, refused the milk of his father's ideology along with his nurse's milk: asked what he had learned, the boy answered that the best of all teachings is devotion to Viṣṇu. Hiraṇyakaśipu tried to destroy him — poison in his milk, serpents in his bed, mantra-hurled weapons, a mountain dropped on his head, a fire fed by sorcery. Each attempt failed as devotion summoned rescue, and the boy emerged unburned, unbitten, unbroken, reciting the names of the god (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5–7.8). The text's power lies in the contrast it never softens: the father holds every worldly power — armies, sorcery, a boon from Brahmā himself — and the son holds only a name, and the name keeps winning. Prahlāda became, for later bhakti theology, the type of the devotee whom nothing can finally injure. His serenity in the face of death is the cycle's quiet, indestructible center — the still point around which all of his father's fury breaks.

myths.title: Out of the Pillar
myths.text: 'Is your Viṣṇu in this pillar?' Hiraṇyakaśipu smashed a golden column of his own palace with his mace — and the pillar answered. From within the masonry came a sound no one in the three worlds had heard before; the column split, and out of it erupted a being that was neither man nor beast: Narasiṃha, the man-lion, maned and roaring, filling the hall with radiance and terror (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19–20). The dying light that streamed through the lattices was neither day nor night. The threshold on which the god seized the tyrant was neither indoors nor out. The claws that disemboweled him were neither weapon nor hand. And the avenger was neither man nor god, neither demon nor beast — exactly the thing for which the boon's careful clauses had never been written. Every condition was honored to the letter and annulled by a form the letter could not imagine. The Purāṇas stage the scene as a trial in which the cosmos itself acts as counsel for the prosecution — and in which devotion, not force, set the whole machinery in motion.

myths.title: The Rage and the Child's Voice
myths.text: Narasiṃha stretched Hiraṇyakaśipu across his thighs and tore him open with his claws, and the three worlds exhaled — but the god's fury did not stop with the killing. His rage blazed until no god dared approach him, until the devas themselves sent the one being the man-lion would not strike: Prahlāda, the child the demon had tried to murder. The boy came unafraid, offering garlands and hymns, and the fire went out of the lion's eyes. Narasiṃha blessed him and granted him the throne of the asuras (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.10; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.20). It is the cycle's deliberate climax: the power that broke a tyrant bows to a child's composure. Later Śaiva tradition complicates the peace — in the Śiva Purāṇa's telling, the burning man-lion is stilled only when Śiva descends as the bird-lion Śarabheśvara and grapples him quiet. The sources openly disagree, and the disagreement fed centuries of Vaiṣṇava–Śaiva debate; that disagreement is itself part of the myth's afterlife.

myths.title: The Nine Lions of the Hills
myths.text: In the Nallamala hills of Andhra Pradesh, local sacred geography multiplies one myth into nine. The Ahobilam tradition knows Nava-Narasimha — nine shrines scattered across forest, cliff, and gorge — where the man-lion is said to have ranged after the killing, each form tied to a rock, a spring, or a cave and each approachable only along the paths of that landscape. The sthala-purāṇas transfer the Purāṇic climax into geology: the god who emerged from architecture at twilight now inheres in the hills themselves, and devotees read the escarpments as his body. The development is transparent and well attested: by the medieval period Narasiṃha had become less a character in one story than a territorial deity whose nine forms guard nine thresholds of the forest. Pilgrimage binds the sites into a single circuit walked in the cool months, turning the Purāṇas' single afternoon in a palace hall into a landscape the devotee must cross on foot — the loophole god, guarding every boundary of his own country.

lore.syncretism: Narasiṃha's afterlife is a study in devotional geography. In South India he became a royal deity: the Vijayanagara court identified itself with Viṣṇu's protective avatāras, and the colossal Ugra-Narasimha at Hampi still shows what the identification looked like in stone. Eastward, Khmer sculptors carved the disemboweling of Hiraṇyakaśipu at Banteay Srei (c. 967 CE), proof that the Purāṇic cycle traveled with Sanskrit culture beyond India. Śaiva tradition answered with the Śarabha episode, in which Śiva must subdue the man-lion's unquenchable rage — a counter-telling that kept Narasiṃha at the center of inter-sectarian argument. In Tantric practice his mantra became standard armor against danger; in vernacular bhakti, Prahlāda's story anchored the claim that devotion outlasts every worldly power.
lore.culturalLegacy: Narasiṃha remains among the most actively worshipped forms of Viṣṇu. Ahobilam's nine shrines and Simhachalam near Visakhapatnam — where the deity is kept under a coat of sandalwood paste renewed annually — anchor major pilgrimage circuits, and Narasimha Jayanti, falling on the full moon of Vaiśākha, celebrates the twilight of the boon. The name itself never left circulation: Narasiṃha, Narasingh, and Narasimhudu serve as given names across India, and new temples — most visibly Yadadri in Telangana — continue to rise around the old story. Modern retellings, from children's comics to cinema, keep returning to the two figures the Purāṇas made unforgettable: the father with the airtight contract, and the son with only a name.
lore.extendedMeditation: Narasiṃha is the divine answer to a lawyer's question: what can kill the man who closed every door? The tradition's answer refuses the terms of the contract — not by breaking it, which would make the god a cheat, but by stepping into the one space the contract could not name: twilight, threshold, claw, man-lion. It is mythology doing what it does at its best, exposing the poverty of exhaustive conditions. The boon fails not because it was poorly drafted but because reality is wider than any list. And the myth's second movement is the greater one: the killing does not end the story — a child's unafraid gentleness does. Between the disemboweled tyrant and the blessed boy, the Purāṇas place the cycle's true thesis: the ferocity that guards the universe is finally governed by, and governs itself for, devotion.

lore.archaeology: The earliest monumental telling of the cycle stands at Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh: Cave 6 (c. 400–401 CE, reign of Candragupta II) carves Narasiṃha disemboweling Hiraṇyakaśipu across his lap — one of the first dated images of the avatāra, and already iconographically complete. The sixth-century Dāśāvatāra temple at Deogarh adds a canonical panel within a full Viṣṇu program. In the far south, Ahobilam's nine shrines in the Nallamala hills embed the myth in living pilgrimage geography. The Vijayanagara capital at Hampi preserves the colossal monolithic Ugra-Narasimha, seated with the demon's body across his thighs, attributed to the early sixteenth century. Outside India, the Banteay Srei temple at Angkor (c. 967 CE) renders the same disemboweling in pink sandstone, with Prahlāda kneeling calmly beside the violence.
